utterances.text: At the local level after the elections there was a division of power based on an agreement reached by the parties that had won the elections, in this case there were three ethnic-based parties, the HDZ, the Serbian Democratic Party, and the Democratic Action Party, wherever at the local level the three parties had participated in the elections. But there were some municipalities, such as Grude, for instance, where only one party actually set up its government because the other parties did not participate in the elections at the local level at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to move on. If we go on to the next chapter which deals with statutory decisions, and that's how we've titled it, and of course this will tie in to your previous testimony concerning your involvement initially on with Livno. The first document is 1D 00155, and of course I'll be discussing in conjunction with this document 1D 00899 and P 00250. So we'll start with these initially. If you look at 1D 00155, it's a decision to create the Croatian Defence Council dated 8 April 1992, and we see that it was published in the Official Gazette, this is known as the Narodni List, on September 1992. Do you recognise this document, sir, and if so when was the first time that you saw it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise this document, and the first time that I saw it was perhaps sometime in early July 1992 in Livno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at Article 2 going back to the previous discussions that we've had, territory areas and what have you, in Article 2 we see that it notes: "Its objective shall be to take care of the sovereign space of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and to protect the Croatian people as well as other peoples in the Community that are attacked by the aggressor." So here we have sort of this new term "sovereign space," but then goes back to "the Community." Can you kind of help us out here a little bit. What -- I understand you didn't draft it, but how is it -- how do you interpret this in light of how it's phrased in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is important to bear in mind that almost a year elapsed between this document and the previous one, and some serious events occurred, the war broke out and there was an aggression on this area. And in essence, this is a response to this aggression, this document I mean, because it is stated here that the sovereignty of this area will be defended and that the Croatian people and other peoples living in this area that has -- had come under an attack, together with Croats, would be defended. So this is an expression of the willingness and readiness to defend the sovereignty of this area against an aggression, the aggression on the part of this party which is trying to take over this area in an aggressive manner, through aggression and violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we look at the next document, 1D 00899, this is dated 15 May 1992, it's a statutory decision. And this -- this is on the provisional - and I emphasize that, provisional - establishment of the executive authority and administration in the territory of the HZ HB, and here I see we have that word, "territory." And if you look at very briefly it talks about Article 1 we see: "... shall carry out the duties of the executive authority ..." this is the Croatian Defence Council, and I guess we would refer to it as HVO HZ HB to make the distinction with the military aspect. And Article 2 we see: "The Croatian Defence Council shall consist ..." and we see that it has a Presidency and the heads of departments. And I don't want to dwell on this too much, but we then see -- the last page we see Mr. Mate Boban who is the president. Do you recall seeing this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I saw this document and several other documents in Livno. It was given to me for my inspection. That was in the context of a radio show where the president of the Executive Board of the Livno municipality was supposed to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I intervene just very briefly since we're now talking about this whole territory and area issue. Could Mr. Karnavas please look at the Croatian translation because there is mention of the word "territory" in the English translation, whereas in the Croatian version the word used is "area," "podrucju." If you look at what it says under the statutory decision, in the Croatian version it says "in the area" and in the English version it says "in the territory." I hope my intervention was premature, but I think it's important at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We appreciate the intervention. I was hoping, I was hoping, and I'll underscore that again, that the witness having the Croatian version would have picked up on that. But that's why I stressed that we saw the word "territory."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So, sir -- because this issue is going to come up again, I guarantee you that. So if you look at the title and if you could please read the title to us so that we at least -- going back where it says "statutory decision" --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you read the rest of it. What does it say? This is 1D 00899.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: It says here in the title that this is a statutory decision on the provisional structure of the executive government and administration in the territory of HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does it use the word "territory" there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the Croatian version the word that is used is "podrucju," area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, what's the word in Croatian? I don't know how it's used by the Serbs or by the Bosniaks, but is this such a word as "territory"; and if so, what would that be?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes -- well, in Croatian there is a word "teritorij," territory, and I tried to explain that, but if you want me to I can do it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure the Judges know that there are those two words because, you know, some things get lost in translation and I just want to make sure when we're talking about area we're not using the word territory, at least not when it's being translated. Okay. Now, you said that you looked at this as a part of a packet of other documents for a radio show, was the other document, the next one, P 00250, which was a statutory decision on municipal executive authority and municipal administration, is that the other document that you were given at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And of course we see that this is 13 June 1992, and we see that Mr. Boban's name -- and he's president of the HVO and, and, the HZ HB. So can we conclude, knowing that it's leading but it's all already in the evidence, can we conclude that at this point Mate Boban is wearing two hats, at least as it appears in this particular document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: We can conclude that at that time Mr. Boban held three functions. He was the president of the HZ HB, he was the president of the Presidency of the HZ HB, and he was the president of the HVO HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And at the time were you able to recognise that when you reviewed these documents for that radio show?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the documents that I had, of course I was able to see that there are several functions held by a single person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's talk about that radio show, let's be brief, let's be concrete. What exactly were you asked to do and what in fact did you do ?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I was asked to go on a local radio and to try and explain this new structure, the new institutions that were set up, the municipal HVOs, the relationship with the HVO HZ HB, and the manner in which those new bodies were supposed to function. And in preparation for this radio programme I tried to do a quick analysis to assist me, and I saw some illogical points in all those decisions and I spoke about them in this radio show and I criticised them because I felt that they were not making this whole system function all that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's just look at just very briefly Article 6, for instance, this might help us a little bit. It says: "The HZ HB HVO shall supervise the legality of the municipal HVO's work." And of course at this point in time we have Mate Boban who is the president of the HZ HB HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you also indicated that he was the president of the Presidency of the HZ HB, and could you please tell us who was sitting -- who made up the Presidency of the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with this decision, the Presidency of the HZ HB comprised leaders of the municipal Croatian Defence Councils, the highest-ranking officials from the ranks of the Croatian people in the municipalities that were not headed by persons of Croat ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in the organizational chart structure, was the HZ HB above or below -- the Presidency, that is, of the HVO? Which one was above, the HZ HB Presidency or the HVO, which of the two?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to say that if you have a single person performing both the functions of the president of the HVO and the president of the Presidency. But formally speaking, the decisions of the HVO were at a lower level than the decisions of the Presidency of the HZ HB. So the HVO was at a lower level than the Presidency. But it is important to note here that in the first stage we're talking about several functions held by the same person, so it is difficult to speak about any conflicts because there were no conflicts between various persons. At that time it was completely immaterial, in my view, whether Mr. Boban signed the decision as the president of the Presidency or as the president of the HVO in terms of its implementation or its significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's because he held all these different positions of authority and power?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, yes, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document which is P 00302, and this is a decision on establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and of course we look at the second page. Here it's signed by the president of the HZ HB, Mate Boban, the date is the 18 of November, 1991, although in the preamble it makes reference to 3 July 1992. And of course there are a couple of things that I would like to discuss. Under reasons, Roman numeral I, if we look at the third paragraph we see the word "unitary state" that -- we see the -- and under the reasons they define the concept of a unitary state unacceptable. In your opinion, what is a unitary -- what is a unitary form of government, the one that's being referred to here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Unitary government in my opinion is the kind of government that does not take into account the fact that there is a multi-ethnic community and some specific features of such a multi-ethnic community when decisions are made, key decisions, within the purview of the state or at any level of government. If we're talking about the unitary model as far as the Croatian people and the Croatian government is concerned at that time, the concept of establishing government in Bosnia and Herzegovina, up until the beginning of the war, was treated as an internal concept, the concept that does not take into account those specific features of a multi-ethnic community that was in existence in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the needs to express the specific interests of this multi-ethnic community through reaching a consensus about key issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just -- and I know that we probably shouldn't be worried too much about this, but today, you living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, working there and what have you, is this concept of this unitary model of government, is that acceptable today or is it still an issue?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: At the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state there are appropriate instruments in place, mechanisms in place, to protect the national interests of each and every constituent people. At the level of the Federation as one of the entities comprising Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is a majority opinion of the Croat people and the Croatian political parties that there is no mechanism in place that would protect the national interests of the Croatian people in an effective manner. Quite often at the federal government and in the federal parliament Croat representatives are out-voted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Or, to put it another way, their representatives are actually voted in by the Bosniaks as opposed to -- in other words, another constituent nation controls the destiny as to who is going to be the Croat leadership at the Presidency or at other levels; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Recent experience has shown that the election so of a representative of the Croat people into the Presidency did not reflect the political will of the Croat people. I don't want to speculate who voted which way because the ballot was a secret one, but it is quite obvious that in the municipalities where Croats have the vast majority, the electoral results do point to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look to Article 7, just to dwell on this a little bit of this document, and we're still on P 00302, we see that the supreme authority is vested first and foremost in the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and then it says to "the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna ..." And then we see, as you indicated earlier, that: "The Presidency shall be the legislative body of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." And if we go to Article 8 which ties in primarily with your previous answers: "The Presidency of the Community shall appoint the executive and administrative bodies of authority of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Now, focusing on these two articles it would appear, at least at this point in time, that Mate Boban is the supreme authority; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: In practical terms what you say is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, again it -- just to drive this point home, lest there be any misconceptions or misunderstandings, if we look at Article 8 and then go back to the previous document we spoke of, that is, P 00250, okay. And of course Article 2 we see in that particular document that the municipal HVO shall consist of the president's and so on and so forth. And then we go to Article 6 and then we see "... the HZ HB HVO shall supervise the legality of the municipal HVO work." And now we see Article 8 in P 00302, it is these - and correct me if I'm wrong - it is these presidents of the municipal HVOs that indeed as a collective body appoint the members of the executive and administrative bodies which they supposedly are to supervise the ones that appointed them and that can dismiss them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer can object if he feels that he needs to object for his colleague, I have no objections for that, but again these are all facts that are well established either through this gentleman's testimony or through previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with your statement. That was precisely what I was criticising, the fact that there is no clear hierarchy in terms of lower- and higher-ranking institutions. This concept implies that presidents of the municipal councils of the HV were members of the Presidency, and then according to this same logic you have a complete system in which everyone answers to everyone else, but essentially no one answers to anyone else. And if you have an authority like that it can't go on working efficiently, and those were the examples that I provided. There should be clear hierarchy in terms of government institutions from the municipal level all the way up to HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, if we go on to the next document, 1D 00156, this is a document, again we've seen this one here in this courtroom, it's dated 3 July 1992. And of course if we look at the trans -- I'm going to read the English version and you tell me if it's correct because I know that you know some English. It says here: "On the temporary" -- this is a: "Statutory decision on the temporary organization and executive authority and administration in the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Which word is used in Croatian, territory or the other word which means area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Area, as in the previous decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we look at Article 9 I think -- because you might be able to help us out a little bit on this one, we've seen this article before, we've heard testimony to that effect because -- but perhaps you might be able to assist us. It says here: "The HVO president shall be in charge of the work of the HVO and shall be held accountable for it, he shall ensure the unity of the political and administrative activities of the HVO, cooperate with other bodies and organizations of the HZ HB, and direct the activities of the HVO as a whole and its members as individuals." Let me begin by asking you first: Was this a collective body that took decisions as a collective or was this the sort of body where the president, for instance, as in many institutions in the West, is above everyone and has veto powers or has the ability to issue decisions irrespective of the will of the rest of the members of the executive?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it's questionable that the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was a collective body. You can see that based on a number of documents, the way they took their decisions. The HVO needs to convene in order to reach a decision by a majority vote, and then the fact that in the document you cite, Article 12 says that each member of the HVO has the right to resign. There is no provision saying that a resignation submitted by the president means a resignation for the HVO as a whole, and this is the way all democratic governments the world over are organized. It is clear based on this that the Croatian Defence Council is working as a collective organ of executive government in these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, because of time we won't discuss any other issues, although the Judges may have some questions on this. But the last document in this area is P 00684, P 00684, dated 17 October 1992, and this is a decision on the amendment of the statutory decision on the provisional organization of the executive power and so on. So this is a decision to amend the one that we just saw. And of course we've seen this one before, just very briefly for the Court's convenience, Article 1 talks about that it can exercise its power to adopt decrees, decisions, dispositions, and conclusions. We see the different definitions. And then we see that it says: "'In cases of suffering -- in cases not suffering delay, the HVO shall adopt enactments falling within the competence of the Presidency of the HZ HB.'" And then of course if we look at the very last paragraph in this article it says: "'The enactments indicated in the preceding paragraph shall be enforced as of the day of their adoption...'" And of course this is of some importance. This is of some importance. So if you could please tell us what exactly is being said here and how should the Judges understand it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: These basic decision empowering the Presidency of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna to adopt normative laws and decrees because of the war situation that was gaining complexity the fact was that members of the Presidency from all corners of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this amendment to the decision empowers members of the Croatian Defence Council in case of deferral to pass norms and laws that would be under the authority of the Presidency of the HZ HB, and then it goes on to state that the HVO must as soon as the conditions are in place submit these documents for approval to the Presidency. Should there be no approval, the laws can no longer be applied. This is about the powers of the members of the Presidency of the HZ HB that are temporarily transferred to the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And again I'm going to have to caution you to speak a little bit slower. First, keeping in mind your answer that you just gave us, if we can go back to the previous document, 1D 00156, and I would like you to focus on Article 18 and I'm doing this although I believe we've already dealt with this issue. I think it's best to sort of hit the nail again on the head until it comes out the other end, as it were. Here we see in 1D 00156 Article 18, it says: "The HVO shall issue decrees, decisions, and conclusions to regulate economic and other relations in the territory of the HZ HB." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we conclude from looking at this particular article that irrespective of the decision of 17 October 1992, there are provisions, earlier provisions, that would allow, at least in this limited area, area regulating economic and other relations, that grant the HVO the authority to issue decrees, decisions, and conclusions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: In a formal and legal sense that is the case, although the fact is we have four different levels of decisions here. Before the Presidency transferred these powers, the HVO could not pass any decrees. Decisions and conclusions, yes, but not decree laws, not before it was empowered to do that by the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if we can go -- just one last sort of housekeeping matter with this P 00684. Again, if we look at the -- where it says "decision on amendment" -- in the title itself, we see the word "territory," is that what is reflected in the Croatian version, is it territory or that other word that we used for -- that denotes area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: This applies to all the documents including the one that we are now talking about. The word is "area" in the original Croatian version of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not pronouncing it because I would like to have it come from the witness's mouth lest there be any complaints that I'm leading him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Karnavas, in the Article 18 you have just referred to we find "territory" but in the original it's also "podrucju."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I could spend my entire six hours dealing with this issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You don't have to, we help you. We help you, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know, I know. Okay. This was not a request for additional time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, if I may, Article 18 in the original Croatian also reads "area," not "territory."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I think Mr. Karnavas is going to proceed to another topic. So I would like to ask a question which in my view is relevant, as indeed all questions I'm going to ask. I would like you to refer to document 1D 00155, it's the third document in the binder. In the preamble of that document, Mr. Karnavas didn't talk about the preamble just before the decision. It's a document dated April the 8th, 1992. Can you see the preamble. Now, I'm going to put the following to you and you will tell me what you think of it. It is a very complicated issue that of the HVO and the Community of Herceg-Bosna was going to spend -- I was going to say hundreds of hours -- at least a lot of time with many witnesses, and you seem to be an appropriate witness to deal with this matter because you have been following closely the drafting of several legal texts. And as a lawyer perhaps you're in better position to answer substance questions. When looking at that document of November the 18th, 1992, establishing the Croatian Defence Council, there is an explanation for the establishment of that community in the preamble, which in English is entitled "reasons." It is stated that pursuant to the constitution the Croatians, which are a constitutive people, like the Serbs and the Muslims, deem it necessary to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg or Herceg-Bosna. This is what you can see these reasons, and reading this paragraph or these reasons, I don't know if everyone shares my point of view, but those who drafted this text think that the 18th of November, legal text is consistent with the constitution, we can say pursuant to the constitution -- so the establishment of that Croatian community takes place because the Croatians within Bosnia-Herzegovina have the impression that their rights are not upheld or respected. And then you have that document of April 18th, 1992, document 155 -- 8th of April, not 18th of April, and the reasons of the preamble is also very interesting because I have a feeling, but I may be wrong, but I have a feeling that the situation has significantly deteriorated because of the Serbian aggressor, as indicated, but also in the preamble or in the reasons it is also stated that the Croatians are no longer protected because of the legal authority has an ability, which is serve the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to secure that protection, to provide that protection, and is also indicated that there is a disintegration, disintegration of the state which can easily be understood and because of that the HVO is to be established. So the situation has obviously deteriorated, hence the HVO is being established in a context which is very different from November. We're talking about a situation in which the Croatians are -- the Croats are no longer protected because under -- according to this text at least there is no more state. So on the basis of your experience, because at the time you were there, I was not there at the time that this was of course -- was thinking about these issue, but according to you in April 1992 has there or was there a deteriorated situation which leads Croats from Bosnia to go one step ahead and establish the HVO because they have to defend themselves? So what do you respond?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer, Mr. President, is a very simple one. Precisely on the day the decision was adopted, what occurred was a disaster for the Croats in Kupres municipality and Kupresko Polje. Over 150 Croats were killed over those two days in the area. The only assistance came from some volunteers who went there and helped those people, but no legal institution in Bosnia and Herzegovina tried to stand up for those people in any way at all. I think it is a tragedy that so many people died, and I think that tragedy alone lends sufficient legitimacy to the Croatian leaders in Bosnia and allows them to conclude that the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at least in Croat-populated areas, had broken down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we conclude that the establishment of the HVO happened for security-related reasons. You mentioned Kupres but there may have been other municipalities where attacks took place. The state of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not present anymore, it was not providing security for its citizens, and is that the reason why the HVO was established? Would I be mistaken in concluding that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, several months prior to this decision a similar tragedy struck the Croats in Trebinje municipality, a village called Ravno. The Croat representatives appealed to the republican bodies of Bosnia and Herzegovina to take some action, because at the time the tragedy struck Bosnia and Herzegovina had not yet been involved in the war in any way. This was yet another negative experience and the conclusion simply suggested itself. There is another thing that was very important. The experience of Kupres and of Ravno showed that areas and municipalities populated by Croats could not stand up for themselves and defend themselves on their own. There was in practical terms a threat that each of these municipalities would be devoured one by one, as the Kupres example showed in no uncertain terms. It was the only logical conclusion that the defence forces should be united. What that meant in practical terms is this: There had to be some joint bodies to coordinate the defence activities. It would have been impossible to defend together in an effective manner unless you had some sort of an HQ that would coordinate all these defensive activities and unite them all under a shared objective or under a common objective. That is my interpretation of the establishment of the Croatian Defence Council. This was a necessity at a time of war, and the idea was perfectly legitimate, to protect the lives and interests of one of the constituent ethnic groups, peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm much obliged. It's an interesting answer, but I do note that at page 72, lines 10 and 11, a clear question is put by Your Honour, "The state of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not present anymore, it was not providing security for its citizens, and is that the reason why the HVO was established? Would I be mistaken in concluding that?" I wonder if the witness can give a yes or no answer to that rather straightforward question for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, you were there in Bosnia and Herzegovina in April 1992 at the time, was there still a state in a position to guarantee the security of its citizens, or was there no more state in that position and is that the reason why some citizens decide -- Croatian citizens decided to set up the HVO? Can you please provide a very straightforward answer to this question because my question was very specific and Mr. Khan has just reminded us of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Unfortunately, there was no state, there were no institutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The establishment of the HVO is something that I see as a necessity, an alternative to this absence of state institutions that might have guaranteed an appropriate defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I come back to a linguistic issue. Here in the preamble we find again the word "territory," but in the Croatian we find neither "territory" nor "podrucju," but "prostor" or "prostori." How would that fall to be translated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, "prostor" also includes whatever is above the ground, the air in this case. This is a possible interpretation. If you have enemy aircraft flying at an altitude of maybe 1 or even 5 metres that lends legitimacy to this, you defend that space, if you like. So this isn't just the ground, the area, it is also the air-space. So if you say "prostor," that includes both, and perhaps also to some degree what is under the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to have a break now. We'll resume at five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Unless there are any other questions from the Bench, we'll move on to the next topic. And this is -- and I've titled this functioning on -- Functioning of HVO HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Perkovic, I'm going to ask you to be as precise and as direct as you can in your answers and rather short. And I'm very grateful to Mr. Khan's intervention. So please listen to my question and please answer it as directly as you can, especially other questions from others as well. All right. 1D 02749. This is dated 8 October 1992. We see it's a request for the submission of a work programme, and we see that it is signed by president of the HVO HZ HB, Dr. Jadranko Prlic, and we see that it's sent off to the various heads of departments. Now, can you -- you've had a chance to look at this. What if anything can you conclude from this particular document in light of the previous documents that we have reviewed here in court today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the HVO wants the head of the department and the head of the commission to submit a proposal of the activities they intend to take within their purview for the period specified herein. So in essence, it is necessary to establish what the activities of the departments and offices are going to be in this time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Who makes that determination, is it the president -- is the president directing them what they should be doing or is it up to the heads of department to figure out what it is that they would be doing? And the reason I'm asking is if we call -- if you recall the Article 9 and the -- in the document 1D 00156, so here I'm trying to tie this in to give sort of a concrete example how we may be able to later on at some point interpret Article 9.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Every head of the department or the chairman of the commission for regulations had to submit a plan of activities for the time-period, his concept of the activities for the relevant time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 01881, and we see that again this is signed by Dr. Jadranko Prlic, dated 20 November 1992. We see that on the second page. A couple of things I want to point out. First, on number 4 it says: "Prior to adopting the Rules, the heads of the departments shall obtain the opinion of the Regulations Commission and the Finance Department, as well as the approval of the HVO of the HZ HB." Who headed the regulation commission and what was that commission about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the head of the commission for regulations were Mr. Vahid Vlahovic [phoen], an attorney-at-law from Mostar, and the purpose of this commission for regulations was to ensure the harmonization of the legislation and other legal instruments passed by bodies and institutions of the HZ HB, and it had yet another task, to participate in the drafting of some legislation because there was a shortage of personnel in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at item number 9 it talks about: "Inspectorates shall be formed to carry out inspectoral supervision within the competence of the administrative body." Were these inspectorates ever appointed and did this activity ever take place to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, primarily because there were not enough experts at the time, the inspectorates were not set up at the time while HZ HB was in existence, although as we can see there was a legal basis for their establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at item number 14 we see that the vice-president of the HVO, Mr. Zubak, is appointed coordinator for matters related to the internal organization of the bodies and services of the HVO HZ HB. If you could please comment and tell us what exactly Mr. Zubak is being appointed to.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this document envisages that the regulations on internal structure will determine the internal structure of each body, each department, of the HVO HZ HB. In essence, it means that this act stipulates the necessary number of employees and the manner in which each institution is going to be set up. It is quite obvious that at that time the role of Mr. Zubak in this context was to coordinate the activities of various departments, taking into account or making sure that when each of these regulations is being implemented that it is done in the same manner, taking into account the pace at which work needs to be done so that it will all -- it should all be implemented within a reasonable time, and to reach compromise when, for instance, the opinions of the heads of the departments and the ministry differed as to the number of personnel needed. And the ministry approved this in light of the funds available for the payroll, to meet the payroll, of all the employees in each of the departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You used the word "ministry." At this point we're talking about departments, and as lawyers we need to be as precise as possible. Ministries may be -- come down the road, so I'm going to be a stickler for that. So I kindly ask you to use the proper terminology when we talk about departments. Now --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, yes, it was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You'll just get a yellow card at this point. Now, the next -- first of all, Mr. Zubak, did he play an important role within the HVO HZ HB; and if so, could you kind of tell us overall, and I know that he's not the main topic of our discussion, but just to introduce this gentleman to the Trial Chamber. What role did Mr. Zubak play, overall that is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zubak was appointed to the post of the vice-president of the Croatian Defence Council of Herceg-Bosna. As far as I can recall, he was one of the two vice-presidents who were -- that were envisaged, and in accordance with our legal tradition in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in accordance with his qualifications and skills, he was an appropriate person to be appointed to that post because of his lengthy experience in administration and the fact that he had a law degree. So he could really do this job, the job that was outside of the economic sphere, the part of the job that had to do with administration proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And before we leave this particular document and in light of the other documents that we have seen, are there any differences that you can see between this sort of system, looking at some of the documents, of course, and the system that existed prior to the elections, as far as procedure and as far as the vision of -- you know, the establishment of collective bodies, governance, and what have you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: In essence, the system is almost identical and this document in a way replicates the documents of Bosnia and Herzegovina, regulating the internal structure of institutions and bodies of government in BH, the ordinance on the internal organization, which is the basic document containing provisions to that effect, the organizational units within each department have virtually identical names, the inspectorate and sections, divisions, and departments. They are terms that were in use in Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At that time --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: -- in legal parlance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go on to the next document, 1D 01181, and this is just for illustrative purposes because we will see other such documents. We see that these are minutes of meeting -- of the 25th meeting, for instance, dated 11 February 1993 for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And we see that you are present, we can see that at the very top. And just, again for illustrative purposes, if we turn to item 3, which would be on page 2 in the English version, it talks about a draft decree on the application of the Law on Employment. And then it says, the second paragraph: "The proposed decree was adopted unanimously, including the following remarks and amendments made by the HVO HZ HB Regulation Commission ..." Can you explain that a little bit to us? What is being said here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: This was the job of the commission for regulations, providing opinions, suggestions, and proposals regarding some certain legal acts that were submitted to it. Departments and other institutions were bound to submit those before the sessions of the HVO HZ HB so that those remarks could be made, taken into consideration, and perhaps built into the final text before the sessions. In this case this was not done because the heads of the departments sometimes insisted on submitting the text of a decision or another act directly to the HVO HZ HB at the session, and then I had to intervene directly and to seek amendments of a certain text right there. And I have to say that in some instances at my insistence the president of the HVO, especially if this could be delayed, the enactment of those legal acts was delayed in order to comply with the requisite procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we discuss what the requisite procedure was at that time, you told us earlier on during our very first session that right after the election when you had been appointed, I believe -- was it assistant in the Ministry of Administration, that you were -- you held a position where you were involved in the drafting of legislation. And I would -- I think we could all benefit if you could kindly tell us the process and the different filters that a piece of legislation would go through. And the reason I'm asking this is because I want to see the difference between what was done then, what was done here, especially since sometimes we tend to look at these legislations -- these pieces of legislation thinking that perhaps all the mechanisms might have been in place so -- and that everything should be harmonised as they should be before adopted. So let's start off with: How would a piece of legislation be drafted and the filters that it would go through before it actually would come into force?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: At the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina this procedure was much more complex than it was in Herceg-Bosna. In Sarajevo, in the republican organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the initial material, a draft of a legal act, was drafted -- was put together by the relevant ministry. This act -- this document was then submitted to the BH government, to the government commissions to be more specific, because there were three commissions at the level of the BH government. In most cases all three of them considered and discussed a legal document of this sort. After that, after it was discussed, it was resubmitted to the relevant ministry which took into consideration all the remarks and then redrafted the document. This legal document or act was then submitted to the government and the government discussed it at its session and then it took the form of a bill, which was then submitted by the government to the parliament. First it was considered by the relevant parliamentary commissions, which then amended it, if necessary, and then it was resubmitted to the government which incorporated all the amendments. And once this bill was amended in this manner, it was then resubmitted to the parliament which then enacted it. And the representatives in the parliament had an opportunity to propose amendments to certain provisions in the law. Once the law was passed or enacted it was submitted to the office -- the legislation office, which then compared the version of the law with the one that was printed out, and it was then submitted by this office to the Official Gazette where it was published. So this was the procedure at the level of the republic. When we're talking about the way in which provisional legal acts in HZ HB were passed, particularly decree laws, in that period, the period while HZ HB was in existence, we had only one level between the department that drafted this legal document and the HVO that passed it. That was the commission for regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Two questions. The first question is: So if we do compare the two, how many layers or filters would a draft go at the republic level and how many layers or filters would it go through at the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: At the level of the republic there were seven filters if I counted them correctly, and at the level of the HZ HB there was only one filter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you describe this method and the procedure at the republic level. Was that before the war and was that, as well, during the war, or did things change?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: The procedure that I described is the procedure that was in place before the war -- and in fact it is the procedure that exists today. But I have to remind you that during the war the BH parliament did not function and that it transferred its powers to another organ, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that it is quite clear that the part of the procedure that took place before the parliament, it could not be done because the parliament was not in session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go now to the next document very quickly, I think we're through with that -- the last one, 1D 00190, and of course 1D 00193, both of these documents if we just look at them very quickly we see that they're both dated 6 January 1993, they're both signed by Dr. Jadranko Prlic. The first one is a decision on the appointment of a Kemal Sabovic. He's appointed the deputy head of department of interior, and then we see Mr. Omica Zukic [phoen], that's in 1D 00193, he's appointed as assistant to the head of department of interior as -- for analysis, information system, and publishing. Now, can you comment on these two documents very briefly, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are documents that show that in the -- that persons of non-Croat ethnic background are appointed to positions in the bodies of HVO HZ HB. We have two persons here of Bosniak ethnicity. I have to say here, I want to say, that in the period -- in this period these were not the only institutions, there was a number of institutions whose personnel was multi-ethnic, particularly at level of the municipalities, the municipal HVO and administration, but in several new institutions of the HZ HB, including the commission that I was in, the commission for regulations, included personnel who were not of Croat ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if you could tell us very briefly, if you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- who proposed the appointments of deputies or assistants in departments, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the department assistants -- department -- assistants to the department heads were recommended by the department heads, but I'm not sure about the deputies, I think they were also recommended by the department heads but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've just something to which I thought Mr. Karnavas would have responded immediately. When you said that in the regulatory commission in which you were, there were also other nationalities than Croats. Could you tell us how many people made up that commission and what was the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 at the time when I became part of the commission, there were three Croats and two Bosniaks in the commission. Later on, in early 1993 all those people, apart from me, left for other jobs. So we had a new composition with three lawyers, two Croats, myself and another female colleague, and there was a third colleague, a female colleague, a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Unless there are any other questions on this topic, I will move on to the next topic which are -- I've titled this Petkovic's drafts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So again to give a sampling of what you were involved. The first document is 1D 0001, and this is a decree on the organization and responsibilities of the departments and commissions of the Croatian Defence Council. We see it's dated 14 August 1992, and we'll start off with this particular document. And first of all, if you could tell us the difference between a department and a commission. Under Article 3 we see it describes a department and a commission, and if you could tell us what was the difference.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: A department is an independent administrative organ headed by an individual who makes decisions and represents this organ. A commission is a collegiate body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at Article 7 it says here in the very first line that: "The department and commissions of the HVO shall cooperate with the republican bodies in the preparation of acts which conform -- confirm the policy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the preparation of laws and other regulations ..." and it goes on. And so my question is -- did this in fact take place? Did the HVO cooperate with republican bodies; and if so, can you give us an example? Mind you, this is now August 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I wrote a draft of this decree during my first stay in Herzegovina in August 1992. Since it was my personal view that the organs of the HZ HB were provisional in nature, as I've already indicated, they were there to defend that area against the aggression. To my view, it was more than logical to stipulate this kind of a solution in Article 7, to state here, in other words, that the departments and the commissions of the HZ HB shall cooperate with the republican organs and so on and so forth because I thought that the organs and institutions of the HZ HB were regional institutions in that area performing that specific function to defend this area against the aggression. I have to say that this draft was tabled at the Presidency of the HZ HB, and when I asked Mr. Buntic whether there were any objections or remarks, he said that it was accepted and adopted unanimously, that there were no objections to it. And I also want to say that throughout the war, while the Croatian Community, and later the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna were in existence, that there was contact between the republican institutions in Sarajevo and the people who sat in the institutions of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I personally was in contact with these people several times, even at the time when the Croat-Muslim, Croat-Bosniak conflict was at its -- at the highest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the second paragraph compels me to ask you a question on this because it has come up before, and I don't want to skip it, though perhaps the Judges will be asking it at their time. It says: "Departments and commissions of the HVO shall cooperate with administrative bodies of other states in the question of common interest, exchanging experience and knowledge, and engaging in other forms of cooperation." And of course any time we see "other states" we have a heightened sense of alertness here because it may give the impression that now the HVO -- HZ HB is going to be interacting at an international level with other states. So could you please comment on this.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: The reality of life in that time called for this paragraph, dictated that this paragraph be included. It is no secret that the units of the Croatian Defence Council and the Croat people in general did receive substantial assistance, financial assistance, material assistance from the Republic of Croatia, food, medical supplies, weapons, and so on. And this paragraph in fact gives legitimacy to the institutions and bodies of the HVO, making it legal for them to cooperate with other bodies, bodies of other states, not only with other bodies of the HVO but with other institutions and bodies that were willing to provide assistance. I have to remind you now that the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina received substantial assistance from the Croatian diaspora, so there had to be contacts with the state authorities in those countries. In particular, when it came to exporting and importing those goods, particularly, for instance, medical supplies and all other kinds of assistance to the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move on to the next document unless there are questions from the Bench. One --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have a short question. Earlier on you said that you had contacts with representatives from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, these are your counterparts taking care of the same things in Sarajevo and elsewhere. I suppose you had contacts by telephone, mail, and did you actually also meet with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already spoke about that one time I got in touch with my colleague, assistant minister of justice, Mr. Halilagic who I met. The other time I was in touch with one of my colleagues was early 1993, it may have been March 1993, I met with Mr. Niaz Skenderovic who was the assistant minister of interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. The third time was at the time or perhaps what constituted the fiercest clashes between the Croats and the Bosniaks. I met in Medjugorje with a member of the BH Presidency who arrived there to see me, Mr. Ivo Komsic. He wanted to see me, and he wanted to try to talk me into returning to Sarajevo since there was a vacant post in the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was meant for a Croat, and I was the next in line based on the election results. Mr. Komsic, as far as I know, is a member of the Supreme Command of the BH army, and as a member of the BH Presidency, spent some time in the area without encountering any particular problems and without any special security system in place, and he spent maybe a total of one or two days in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These three contact persons you sought, did they see you as people working in total -- in a total illegal situation or did they view you as their counterparts, something that would expect having a counterpart -- in other words, what was their attitude? Were they hostile? Did they work in a spirit of cooperation or were they just neutral towards you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my personal experience, the contacts were, to say the least, cordial. Those persons came to this area, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I noticed absolutely no animosity on their part, although of course they knew where I worked and what my job was. Our talks were perfectly normal, although there is an important fact that I must point out. It was the nature of my work, and I was working with the regulation commission at the time, I was probably among the people who had the least contacts of that nature, people working across the various departments were probably encountering more opportunities to meet all sorts of people working with the BH administration. My own experience, based on these contacts, was very positive and satisfying in every way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And picking up from that question, were others having contacts or were you the only one that was having contacts at the republic level or those who were in Sarajevo working in the -- what I would call the Sarajevo government?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I don't have my records with me here, needless to say, but as far as I know most of the heads of other departments enjoyed contacts like these with their counterparts from the Sarajevo administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move through a series of documents. Hopefully we're going to conclude this chapter tonight, and the first document is 1D 00014 and it's a decree on stamps. One may say, Well, what does that have to do with the events here? However, we need to make sure that we fully understand the concept of a stamp or a seal. And so, can you please tell us how seals or stamps were used and what significance did they play?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: Seals are relatively important in our legal tradition, the legal tradition of Bosnia and Herzegovina and other former Yugoslav republics. Quite simply, the local population was used to believing that no serious legal document would lack a seal or a stamp as well as a signature. There would always have to be a stamp by the appropriate institution, belonging to the appropriate institution, and that is why this decree was important to us because here we defined the procedure for this, what a stamp or a seal should look like, a stamp or a seal used by the institutions of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just phrase it slightly differently. In light of what you just told us, should the Trial Chamber draw any conclusions that simply because seals were used, and the whole concept was introduced by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that somehow the use of the seal is indicative of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna of being some sort of an entity, a para-state, a state within a states, something that is outside Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or at least attempting to be outside?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is nothing but logical to draw such a conclusion. I have explained to you what the main motive was, the main reason, for these stamps to be made. I do have to say that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna saw itself as a state or some sort of a state, or rather, had it seen itself as some sort of a state, then the name of this decree would have been somewhat different because in our legal tradition, in the legal tradition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are laws on stamps, stamps containing what we refer to as the state's coat of arms, and then there's a procedure in place relating to these stamps. In this decree we're not discussing any stamp or seal containing the coat of arms in Bosnia-Herzegovina, although Bosnia-Herzegovina actually had a coat of arms. We are simply talking about the fact that there are appropriate institutions that prove the authenticity of their documents in addition to the signature of whoever is in charge by putting a stamp on these same documents. This is first and foremost a question of our legal tradition. This tradition is still alive and well. We live in an electronic age and we are encountering serious problems in Bosnia-Herzegovina in terms of communicating by e-mail or passing documents and laws by e-mail because the population still wants to see hard copies with stamps on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if I -- just for technical purposes, you begin the answer, at least it's been translated as such based on my question: "I think it is nothing but logical to draw such a conclusion." In English that would mean that it is logical to draw the conclusion of which -- and as I see the rest of your answer, I believe what you're attempting to say that it is not logical to draw such a conclusion, the one that I was referring to in my question. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does everybody see that, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there is something I have seen which I want you to clarify because this may have consequences. We have understood that people like to have a document with seals. This is the case for all countries of the world; it is nothing specific to your country. But if that is something -- it may be a lapse of the tongue or something else, but I heard you say that the Croats considered themselves as a state, does that mean that they considered Herceg-Bosna as a state or was it an entity within the state that was the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Could you clarify this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I said this, in keeping with this tradition, the population expected the organs of government performing the functions of the government, regardless of the level involved, to endorse their laws and documents by stamping them in addition to having a signature there, the signature of whoever represents these authorities in terms of signing the laws or documents. Needless to say, no conclusion can be based or drawn based on this, and that is why I was saying that this is something that brings to mind a state, because all the organs of government in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the municipal ones, the republican ones, have a stamp. It doesn't mean that when this decree on stamps was adopted the intention was to display such an interest in a way that would be similar to the way of a state or a para-state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, the passage concerned at lines 10 and following of page 90 are indeed a bit confusing when one reads the whole paragraph or the first half of it. A possibility to interpret what you said or are recorded as having said, "I think it is nothing but logical to draw such a conclusion." That was a quotation. Could that be understood or did you want to say it would be logical, it would be logical, to conclude in that way but in fact the conclusion would be wrong? I see Ms. Tomanovic is shaking her head.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You had no translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just trying to say, I would like to ask Mr. Perkovic again to slow down with his answers because the interpreters, they're obviously encountering a lot of difficulty interpreting him. The entire answer does not make sense to you; it only made sense to us who understand the language. Maybe Your Honour, Mr. Antonetti, should re-ask that particular --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear Ms. Tomanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 90, lines 10 through 25 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear Ms. Tomanovic on account of the background noise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to try and rephrase the question. When a -- so a document with a stamp as defined in this decree would be considered logical to have a stamp next to the signature or - and listen very carefully to my question - or did he think that this document had been issued by a state which was Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to simplify this for my answer to the greatest extent possible in order to put my point across. We have the decree on stamps. It provides for the right for the institutions of Herceg-Bosna to use a stamp. That stamp in terms of its form or physical appearance never refers to Herceg-Bosna as a state, the Republic of Herceg-Bosna as a state. In keeping with our tradition it cannot be concluded that the possession of a stamp by any institution by default implies an association with a state organ or a state. I think I have been very clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, this was very clear. Another question. We've gone through thousands of documents, myriads of documents, of all nature, of all kinds, some of them signed by Mr. Prlic and by others. Now, there was conflict, there was a war going on, military actions taking place. Now, from the outside, in our position as Judges, we are wondering how it could have been possible in such situations to take the time to sign a document. Earlier on we reviewed a document appointing two people and -- to two commissions, where there was -- when there was a crisis. Was it to do with bureaucracy, with the tradition in your country, or was the situation such that it was possible to process this heap of documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in relation to the total number of normative acts in the legal system of a community or a country, the number of acts that were adopted over this period of duration, practically four years, may not be relatively great. I would like to remind you that those acts were adopted that at the time were believed to be necessary. A series of very important laws were never passed by Herceg-Bosna; rather, they were simply taken over directly by Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather, the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina were applied such as, for example, the Law on Inheritance or the Law on Binding Relations or the Law on Family and so on and so forth. These are all systematic laws in a country, and they were directly applied throughout the HZ HB, or rather, HZ HR HB, and this applied throughout the period of time that I'm talking about. Obviously this was about taking over those regulations, or rather, adopting those regulations that were believed to be absolutely necessary with no more than a modicum of potential in terms of human resources or financial means. I told you about my commission, it was a commission comprising three members and we had a typewriter that was hardly in good working order and the room was no more than 5 square metres, the room that we had to work, it was under such conditions that these institutions had to perform their work. They probably would have never started drafting any regulations that weren't in one way or another deemed necessary in terms of organizing daily life in the area. For example, a child goes through the first four years of elementary school, and then you want to issue this child with a certificate on successful completion of the first four years, the programme, what stamp are you going to use in order to certify this for the benefit of this child? Two young people want to get married. As proof of their marriage you would like to be able to issue a marriage certificate. How will you prove that the marriage is valid and how are they going to prove this in the future unless the marriage is actually certified in such a way? Nevertheless, it is the republican -- the regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina that set forth this obligation to certify these documents. There, there are a series of such examples from daily life about the need for this procedure to be prescribed, how stamps are made, and this can't just boil down to some sections of the HVO, departments of the HVO, or institutions, state authorities in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer. It's already past the time -- Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just have one question for Judge Trechsel. If his question was -- if he's satisfied with the question -- you had a question to the gentleman. If you're satisfied, or do I need to worry about it overnight and revisit the issue. There's a great deal of anxious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Let's both worry overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, okay, if you're insufficient with the answer, please ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think I leave it at that. I have not now been impatiently waiting for that answer. So I must confess that I have let myself be drawn along with the course of the proceedings, and I would not -- if I want to come back to it, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then I guess we'll see each other at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, you are to appear before us again tomorrow at 9.00 a.m. we'll have a break around half past 12.00 for us to be able to have lunch and we'll resume in the afternoon. Have a pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of September, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
